segments.say: Here's a thought that might be rather comforting. While you lie there, perhaps nearly asleep, doing nothing at all, there is a quiet team at work in your head. They aren't dreaming up anything dramatic. They're tidying, sorting, and filing the day.

People have suspected for a very long time that sleep helps memory. But suspecting something and showing it are different things. The first careful experiment on the question was done a hundred years ago, in a laboratory at Cornell University.

In 1924, John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had two volunteers learn lists of nonsense syllables. Then they tested them after one, two, four or eight hours. Sometimes the volunteers slept through the interval, and sometimes they stayed awake and went about their day. Memory was clearly better after sleep.

show.what: Tested memory for nonsense syllables after hours spent asleep or awake

segments.say: The researchers drew a thoughtful conclusion. Forgetting, they wrote, seems to be less a matter of old impressions simply fading with the clock, and more a matter of new experience getting in the way. A sleeping mind meets less new experience, and that may be a gentler way to spend the hours.
So what is happening in there? To answer that, scientists had to listen to individual brain cells.

In 1994, Matthew Wilson and Bruce McNaughton recorded the activity of many individual hippocampal cells in rats. While a rat ran around a track, certain cells fired when it was in certain places, so the pattern of cells traced the journey. Then the rat slept. And the cells that had fired together during the run tended to fire together again in sleep.

show.what: Recorded from many hippocampal cells in rats while they ran along a track, and again while they slept

segments.say: Later work showed that the replay can happen at a faster pace than the original experience, as if the day were being fast-forwarded. In 2007, Daoyun Ji and Matthew Wilson showed that this replay was coordinated between the hippocampus and the visual cortex, which hints at a conversation between the quick learner and the slower storage areas.

A common view, set out by Susanne Diekelmann and Jan Born in 2010, is that sleep supports consolidation. Patterns from the day are replayed. The links that matter are strengthened. The memory leans toward the cortex. And in one popular idea, called synaptic homeostasis, sleep also turns down the noise, making room for tomorrow.

show.title: What the night shift seems to do
items: Moves the memory toward the cortex

segments.say: That last idea has supporters and critics, and the details are still being worked out. And while the broad picture, that sleep helps memory, has a lot of support, scientists continue to argue about exactly which stage of sleep does which job. It's a lively research area, which is a good reason to be modest about it.
Here's one of the strangest experiments in this field, and it comes with a lovely smell.

In 2007, Björn Rasch and colleagues asked volunteers to learn where cards were hidden on a grid, while a faint rose scent was in the room. Then, during deep sleep, some of the volunteers were given the same scent again. When they woke, those who had smelled the rose in their sleep remembered the card positions better than those who had not.

show.who: Björn Rasch, Christian Büchel, Steffen Gais & Jan Born
show.what: Used a rose scent while people learned, and again during deep sleep

segments.say: It's important to be clear about what this does and doesn't show. The scent didn't teach anyone anything new. They had learned the cards while awake. It seems that the scent reminded the sleeping brain of that learning, and nudged the replay along. You can't learn French by playing it while you sleep.
From the outside, a sleeping person looks like they're doing nothing. From the inside, at least some of the time, there's a great deal going on. The room is still. The brain isn't idle.

show.cap: A quiet room, and a busy brain

segments.say: What about the opposite? What if the night shift is short?

In 2007, Seung-Schik Yoo and colleagues kept volunteers awake all night, and the next day scanned their brains as they tried to memorise pictures. Compared with rested volunteers, the sleepless group remembered fewer of the pictures, and the hippocampus was less active as they tried. A tired brain seems to find it harder to take new things in.

show.what: Kept people awake for a night, then scanned their brains while they tried to memorise pictures

segments.say: So sleep seems to help twice. It helps to prepare the brain to take in new things, and it helps to settle what's already there. It's why a student's all-nighter is rather a poor bargain. They've swapped a night of consolidation for a few more hours with the book, and a tired brain that finds it harder to make new memories.

Now, if you're someone who sometimes struggles to sleep, please don't take this as one more thing to worry about. One bad night will not undo your memory, and worrying about sleep tends to make sleep harder. These are averages, over groups of people, and your brain is more forgiving than the headlines make it sound.

Some studies suggest that even a short nap can help a memory settle. The evidence there is a bit more mixed, and the effects tend to be smaller than for a full night. But it's a gentle reminder that rest isn't a waste of time. In a way, it's part of the work.
Sleep seems to help more than facts. It also seems to polish skills, and this is where the evidence is perhaps strongest.

In 2002, Matthew Walker and colleagues taught people a short sequence to tap with their fingers on a keyboard, as quickly and accurately as possible. When they were tested twelve hours later, those who had slept in between had improved by about a fifth, while those who had stayed awake had not. The practice had improved overnight.

show.what: Taught people a finger-tapping sequence, then tested them after a night's sleep or after a day awake

segments.say: It fits a pattern many musicians and athletes report. You struggle with a passage on Monday, and on Tuesday it's easier, as if your fingers had been practising in the night. In a sense, they had. The motor memory seems to have been refined while you slept.

In 2003, Sara Mednick, Ken Nakayama and Robert Stickgold tested a visual learning task, where people got faster at spotting a pattern. A nap of an hour or so, containing deep sleep, produced gains in the afternoon that were similar to the gains seen after a whole night. It suggests that a short rest can sometimes do part of the work.

show.who: Sara Mednick, Ken Nakayama & Robert Stickgold
show.what: Compared a nap of an hour or so with a full night, on a visual learning task

segments.say: None of this means you have to do anything special. It's simply a gentle reminder that the hours of rest we sometimes feel guilty about are hours in which the brain is quietly practising. And that you can trust it to carry on.
Sleep may help with more than keeping things. It may help us see something new in them.

In 2004, Ullrich Wagner and colleagues gave volunteers a long, tedious number task which had a hidden shortcut that made it much quicker, if you spotted it. After a first session, they were left for eight hours, either awake or asleep. After a night of sleep, people were more than twice as likely to find the shortcut as those who stayed awake.

show.who: Ullrich Wagner, Steffen Gais, Hilde Haider, Rolf Verleger & Jan Born
show.what: Gave people a number puzzle with a hidden shortcut, and tested whether they found it after a night's sleep

segments.say: It lends some scientific weight to the old advice to sleep on a problem. The idea is that, while you rest, the brain reorganises what it has learned, and sometimes it finds a connection that your tired, busy daytime mind could not see. It doesn't happen every time. But it is a lovely thought.
So that's the third stop. New memories need time and quiet to settle. The sleeping brain replays the day. Different stages of sleep seem to do different jobs. And rest before learning helps too.

show.title: The third stop
items: New memories need time and quiet to settle
The sleeping brain replays the day
Stages of sleep seem to do different jobs

segments.say: So, after a night of this kind of tidying, where exactly is your Tuesday dinner? Where does a memory actually live? For decades, scientists went looking for it, and what they found is both disappointing and wonderful.
